hook.text: Most engines use the Otto cycle, but hybrids rely on a 19th-century trick called the Atkinson cycle.

buildup.text: Atkinson engines hold the intake valve open longer, letting some air escape before compression.

discovery.text: This makes the expansion stroke longer than compression, extracting more energy per fuel drop.

twist.text: The trade-off is less peak power—but electric motors fill the gap perfectly in hybrid cars.

climax.text: Toyota's Prius popularized the Atkinson cycle, proving efficiency could outsell raw power.

punchline.text: Letting air escape on purpose makes the engine more efficient.

quiz.question: Why is the Atkinson cycle more efficient than the Otto cycle?
options: It uses less fuel per injection
Its expansion stroke is longer than compression

details.summary: The Atkinson cycle keeps intake valves open longer during compression to reduce the effective compression ratio while maintaining a long expansion stroke, extracting more energy per combustion event at the cost of reduced peak power.
details.whyItMatters: The Atkinson cycle is used in virtually every hybrid car because its high efficiency pairs perfectly with an electric motor that compensates for its lower power output during acceleration.
takeaways: Intake valves stay open longer, reducing effective compression
The expansion stroke is longer than the compression stroke
Toyota Prius and most hybrid engines use the Atkinson cycle

faq.question: Why is the Atkinson cycle more efficient than the Otto cycle?
faq.answer: By expanding gases further than they were compressed, the engine extracts more work from each combustion event. The longer expansion stroke converts more thermal energy to mechanical work, reducing waste heat.

faq.question: Why is the Atkinson cycle not used in all engines?
faq.answer: The trade-off is significantly less power per unit of displacement. Non-hybrid cars using Atkinson cycle engines feel sluggish during acceleration. In hybrids, the electric motor fills this power gap perfectly.
